project_and_compatibility.implementation_language: Puppeteer, Vitest, and Jest are implemented primarily in TypeScript and run on Node.js. E2E tests can be authored in TypeScript or JavaScript with Puppeteer's bundled type declarations. This evaluation uses Puppeteer with Vitest as the preferred composition and treats Jest as a viable runner alternative.
project_and_compatibility.node_and_typescript_compatibility: Puppeteer 25.8.0 requires Node.js >=22.12.0, documents TypeScript >=5.0.1 and ES2022 or later, and publishes ESM with bundled declarations. Vitest 4.1.11 supports Node ^20, ^22, or >=24 and ships TypeScript/ESM support; Jest 30.4.2 supports Node >=24 but TypeScript normally adds Babel or ts-jest and native ESM remains more configuration-heavy. The repository's Node 24.12 and TypeScript 6.0.3 satisfy the declared ranges. [uncertain] No repository-local type-check and execution spike verified Puppeteer 25.8.0 plus Vitest 4.1.11 against this exact TypeScript 6 configuration.
project_and_compatibility.operating_system_support: Puppeteer supports Windows x64, macOS x64/arm64, and Debian/Ubuntu or Fedora/openSUSE Linux x64 for Chrome for Testing; Firefox follows Mozilla platform requirements. Local x64 Linux and GitHub-hosted Ubuntu x64 are suitable. Official Chrome for Testing Linux support is x64 in Puppeteer's system requirements, and an open project task still tracked Linux arm64 documentation, so arm64 Linux should not be assumed for the standard downloaded Chrome artifact.
project_and_compatibility.license_and_governance: Puppeteer is Apache-2.0 and is led by Google's Chrome browser-automation team in a public GitHub organization. Vitest is MIT, community-developed with public team and OpenCollective information, and its site identifies VoidZero Inc. and contributors. Jest is MIT and governed under the OpenJS Foundation. These licenses permit repository and CI use without a paid service; normal license and notice obligations remain.
project_and_compatibility.installation_model: Preferred baseline: npm install --save-dev puppeteer vitest. Puppeteer postinstall downloads a version-matched Chrome for Testing of about 282 MB on Linux and chrome-headless-shell into $HOME/.cache/puppeteer; Firefox is skipped by default and can be enabled in Puppeteer configuration followed by npx puppeteer browsers install. Linux browser libraries and unzip are required, and Firefox extraction needs xz or bzip2. The alternative is puppeteer-core with a separately managed browser. Jest would replace Vitest and may add @jest/globals plus a TypeScript transformer. A versioned ghcr.io/puppeteer/puppeteer image is available.
project_and_compatibility.candidate_scope_and_layer: A composed browser-automation stack, not a complete E2E framework. Puppeteer supplies browser control, locators, contexts, network events, screenshots, video, and low-level tracing; Vitest or Jest supplies discovery, assertions, hooks, retries, workers, and reports. Application lifecycle, database fixtures, visual baselines, and integrated failure bundles remain project-owned.
project_and_compatibility.authoring_and_async_model: Tests use ordinary TypeScript or JavaScript with native async/await. The preferred API combines Vitest describe/test/expect and typed fixtures with Puppeteer Browser, BrowserContext, Page, and Locator objects. There is no command queue or required DSL. Every Puppeteer promise must be awaited, and helper fixtures should centralize browser/context creation, page cleanup, synchronization, and failure artifacts.
project_and_compatibility.build_pipeline_coupling: Puppeteer is black-box browser automation and can navigate to the Parcel development server or the production Parcel output served by Gin without transforming application source. Vitest uses Vite to transform E2E test modules, but that Vite dependency is confined to the test runner and does not replace or instrument the application's Parcel pipeline. Jest can avoid Vite but needs its own TypeScript/ESM transform configuration. Neither option requires a production frontend build change.
project_and_compatibility.testability_instrumentation_required: No injected runtime, special browser script, relaxed content-security policy, or frontend build hook is required. Existing labels, roles, text, IDs, and CSS can drive the application. Stable data-test attributes are optional where templates lack unique semantic selectors. Deterministic API seed/reset facilities and a controlled Yahoo Finance boundary may still be needed for reliable tests, but those are application testability concerns rather than Puppeteer requirements.

Firefox stable support has been production-ready since Puppeteer 23. Puppeteer follows the latest maintenance Node LTS and releases in lockstep with browsers, which can require frequent runtime and package upgrades. [uncertain] No long-horizon public product roadmap or formal succession plan was found, so protocol transition and future Node support horizons should be reviewed during upgrades.
maintenance_health.dependency_currency: Puppeteer 25.8.0 requires Node >=22.12, was published with Node 24.15, and pins puppeteer-core 25.8.0, @puppeteer/browsers 3.2.1, chromium-bidi 17.0.2, and current protocol data. Its repository rolled Chrome 152 and Firefox 154 immediately before observation. Vitest 4.1.11 directly supports Node 24 and Vite 6-8; Jest 30.4.2 declares Node 24 support. This is current enough for the repository's Node 24.12 and TypeScript 6 baseline.
maintenance_health.wrapper_upstream_lag: There is no Puppeteer wrapper lag when Vitest or Jest calls Puppeteer directly; the browser library and its managed revisions are released together, while the runner is protocol-agnostic. The optional jest-puppeteer preset is a separate community wrapper: version 11.0.0 was published in December 2024 with a broad puppeteer >=19 peer range. Avoiding that preset and owning a small fixture removes its release-lag risk. Vitest requires no Puppeteer adapter.
maintenance_health.maintainer_concentration: Google/Chrome organizational backing and multiple recent human contributors reduce abandonment risk, while Vitest and Jest have separate active organizations. npm metadata for Puppeteer lists only one individual account and one Google publishing account, and releases/browser rolls are heavily automated. [uncertain] Current write-access membership, review distribution, funding allocation, and a formal succession plan were not available, so the Puppeteer-specific human bus factor cannot be quantified.

[uncertain] Exact contributor and dependency-graph dependent counts were not captured, and runner repository metrics cover much broader testing use than this E2E composition.
community_adoption.ecosystem_usage: Puppeteer has extensive use in browser automation, testing, scraping, rendering, and tooling; official Chrome DevTools Recorder workflows and Puppeteer Replay can produce or replay automation. Jest publishes an official Puppeteer integration guide, while Vitest's generic typed fixtures compose directly without an adapter. Maintained adjacent packages include @axe-core/puppeteer 4.13.0, image comparison libraries, CI reporters, and integrations from browser-cloud vendors. These integrations are useful but do not constitute one unified E2E lifecycle.
community_adoption.community_support: Versioned official Puppeteer documentation covers installation, browser management, locators, network interception, debugging, Docker, protocols, and APIs. Support material is available through an active GitHub tracker, the large Stack Overflow puppeteer tag, Chrome Developers channels, and extensive third-party examples. Vitest and Jest both provide mature runner documentation and community channels. Puppeteer's GitHub repository does not enable Discussions, so issue and external-forum support are more important.

Vitest rose about 5.74 times and Jest about 1.31 times over their matching windows. Same-week development and nearly 95,500 Puppeteer stars reinforce continued interest, while downloads remain installation traffic rather than unique teams.
community_adoption.adoption_metric_normalization: The primary browser-layer metric is the direct npm package puppeteer, all versions, for 2026-08-14 through 2026-08-20, compared with the identical package and calendar dates in 2025. It includes CI reinstalls, transitive dependencies, bots, scraping, PDF generation, and non-test automation, so it overstates E2E adoption. Vitest and Jest counts are reported separately and mostly represent unit/integration testing unrelated to Puppeteer. GitHub Puppeteer metrics cover its whole browser-automation project, not this exact stack.

browser_and_runtime_coverage.browser_engines: Official first-class targets are Chrome for Testing and stable Firefox. Chrome/Chromium installations can be selected through executablePath or supported channels, but compatibility is guaranteed for the revision paired with the Puppeteer release. There is no WebKit or native Safari target and no first-class Edge project. This is broader than historical Chrome-only Puppeteer but materially narrower than a Chromium/Firefox/WebKit framework.
browser_and_runtime_coverage.browser_protocol: Chrome uses Chrome DevTools Protocol by default. Firefox uses WebDriver BiDi by default, and Chrome can opt into WebDriver BiDi. Puppeteer documents that Chrome remains on CDP by default because not every CDP feature is available through BiDi; unsupported BiDi operations throw UnsupportedOperation. CDP provides deep Chrome control but is browser/version-coupled, while BiDi improves cross-browser standardization as its implementation matures.
browser_and_runtime_coverage.headless_and_headed_modes: Chrome for Testing and Firefox can run headless in CI or headed for local diagnosis. Chrome for Testing uses the same modern browser path for headed and default headless modes; the older chrome-headless-shell is separately available with headless set to shell. Puppeteer defaults to headless and supports headless false, slowMo, and DevTools for interactive debugging.
browser_and_runtime_coverage.browser_version_management: The puppeteer package downloads a tested Chrome for Testing revision and chrome-headless-shell into a configurable global cache; Firefox can be enabled and downloaded through configuration. Versions are mapped to Puppeteer releases, and updating Puppeteer may require a new browser download. puppeteer-core skips downloads for system or remote browser management. Deterministic CI should pin the package/lockfile and image or browser cache rather than use latest or an auto-updated executable.
browser_and_runtime_coverage.parallel_browser_support: Puppeteer can launch multiple browsers, pages, or contexts, but it has no browser-project matrix or test scheduler. Vitest projects, workers, maxWorkers, fileParallelism, and native file sharding can supply those controls; Jest offers projects, workers, and sharding. The harness must map each runner project to Chrome or Firefox configuration, name artifacts by browser, cap concurrent browser processes, and allocate database state safely.
browser_and_runtime_coverage.mobile_emulation: Puppeteer provides KnownDevices and Page.emulate for device viewport and user-agent presets, plus viewport, touch, device scale, geolocation, orientation-related metrics, and low-level CDP controls. This supports responsive and mobile-like Chrome testing, not physical Android/iOS execution. Some emulation functions are protocol/browser-specific and should not be assumed identical under Firefox BiDi.
browser_and_runtime_coverage.real_browser_fidelity: The managed targets are real Chrome for Testing and stable Firefox binaries rather than generic in-process DOM simulators. Chrome for Testing is designed for automation and tracks Chrome code, and current Firefox support uses stable releases. No execution here represents Apple Safari: neither Chrome nor Firefox is WebKit, and even a generic WebKit build would not be equivalent to Safari's macOS packaging and integrations.
browser_and_runtime_coverage.environment_determinism_controls: Puppeteer exposes viewport/device descriptors, user agent, locale, timezone, geolocation, permissions, media type/features such as reduced motion, color scheme, network/offline and CPU conditions, cache control, and script/style injection. BrowserContext isolates cookies and local storage. There is no integrated cross-browser test clock or seeded randomness fixture equivalent to a complete runner's deterministic environment; clock, Math.random, animations, backend time, and server randomness require evaluateOnNewDocument, CDP, CSS, application configuration, or custom fixtures.

application_fit.dynamic_dom_synchronization: Puppeteer Locators are a good but incomplete fit for HTMX swaps. They retain a query rather than a stale ElementHandle, wait for presence, visibility, enabled state, viewport placement, and a stable bounding box, and can retry an action. Lower-level waitForSelector and stored handles do not retry detached actions. Puppeteer supplies no web-first assertion library, so tests must pair locators with waitForFunction, DOM/response predicates, or Vitest expect.poll and assert a specific post-swap state rather than rely on sleeps or blanket network idle.
application_fit.routing_support: Page.goto, url, goBack, goForward, reload, waitForNavigation, and waitForFunction can exercise direct Navigo deep links and history transitions. Because pushState routing may not create a document navigation, the harness should wait for the expected URL and a route-specific DOM condition instead of always using waitForNavigation. A fresh BrowserContext/page and explicit route cleanup prevent history and storage leakage between tests.
application_fit.locator_model: Recommended locators support CSS plus Puppeteer text, XPath, ARIA name/role, shadow-DOM piercing, filters, and custom query handlers. ARIA selectors use the browser accessibility tree and are preferable for labels and controls. Puppeteer does not provide the same dedicated getByRole/getByLabel/test-id vocabulary or strict single-match failure behavior as leading integrated E2E runners; selectors that match multiple elements need an explicit uniqueness convention, and ElementHandles must not be retained across HTMX replacement.
application_fit.form_interaction: Locator fill, click, hover and scroll plus Page/ElementHandle focus, select, type, keyboard, mouse, touchscreen, and real Tab/click interactions cover focus, blur, input, change, native validation, and dynamic rows. Locator fill chooses behavior by input type. Hidden synchronized values can be inspected through evaluate, while script-setting fields should be avoided because it bypasses user behavior. Dynamic rows require locator reacquisition and an explicit DOM-ready assertion.
application_fit.canvas_and_download_support: Chart.js canvas can be checked through visible legends/labels, application data, page.evaluate inspection of Chart.js state or pixel data, screenshots, and a project-selected image diff library; semantic/data assertions should remain primary. Puppeteer's official files guide states that downloads cannot currently be handled programmatically. Chrome download behavior or raw CDP plus filesystem polling can direct and detect files, but filename, completion, payload verification, cleanup, and cross-browser behavior are custom and materially weaker than an integrated Download object.
application_fit.network_and_api_access: Puppeteer exposes request, response, request-failed, console, and page-error events; waitForRequest/waitForResponse; and request interception with abort, continue, or respond. Enabling interception stalls every request until handled and asynchronous handlers require careful resolution checks. Node fetch can seed/reset REST fixtures. Browser-originated Yahoo requests can be intercepted, but server-side Gin Yahoo access needs an application-side stub, proxy, or configuration because browser interception cannot observe backend egress.
application_fit.same_origin_support: The browser can target the consolidated production Gin origin or Parcel's development origin and existing API proxy without source injection or CORS changes. A BASE_URL fixture is sufficient. If tests or browsers run in containers, localhost is container-relative, so the harness must use published host ports, a host-gateway mapping, or shared Compose networking.
application_fit.test_isolation: Puppeteer BrowserContexts isolate cookies and local storage and can be created per test; pages and contexts must be closed manually in fixture cleanup. Vitest 4.1 typed fixtures can create test-, file-, or worker-scoped resources and register cleanup. Browser isolation does not isolate PostgreSQL, so state-mutating tests still need unique data, a reset API, separate schemas/databases, or serial execution. A browser can be worker-scoped while each test receives a fresh context and page.
application_fit.external_server_model: Puppeteer naturally targets any independently running HTTP server. A configurable base URL can point at Parcel development, the production Compose stack, or a deployed environment. Neither Puppeteer nor Vitest/Jest provides a Playwright-style webServer coordinator, so process launch, dynamic ports, HTTP readiness, and service teardown need scripts, global setup, or CI steps.
application_fit.application_lifecycle: Vitest global setup and typed fixtures, or Jest globalSetup/globalTeardown and a custom environment, can invoke the build, start Docker Compose, wait for Flyway/backend readiness, and tear down. The repository's Compose dependencies already gate the backend on healthy PostgreSQL and successful migration. The stack still needs a repository-owned process wrapper for readiness polling, disposable volumes, fixture seeding, cancellation signals, log capture, and guaranteed docker compose down --volumes; Puppeteer only owns browser lifecycle.
application_fit.visual_regression_workflow: Puppeteer provides page/element screenshots but no baseline store, update command, masking, tolerance policy, per-browser snapshot paths, diff viewer, or CI review flow. Vitest/Jest snapshots do not turn screenshots into a complete visual workflow without a matcher and image-diff library. The project must add tools such as pixelmatch or an image-snapshot matcher, stabilize fonts/OS/browser/viewport/data/time/animations, retain expected/actual/diff images, and keep separate Chrome/Firefox baselines. Deterministic Chart.js data and completed animations are mandatory.
application_fit.accessibility_audit_integration: Deque's maintained open-source @axe-core/puppeteer 4.13.0 injects axe into frames and returns violations suitable for Vitest/Jest assertions and reports. Puppeteer also exposes accessibility-tree inspection and ARIA locators. There is no integrated ARIA-snapshot assertion/reporting workflow in this composition, so reusable audit fixtures, exclusions, attachments, and human-readable output require harness code. Automated axe checks still cover only part of accessibility.

reliability.waiting_model: Locator actions wait for presence and applicable viewport, visibility, enabled, and stable-bounding-box conditions and may retry before acting. Explicit primitives include locator.wait, waitForSelector, waitForFunction, waitForNavigation, waitForRequest/Response, and waitForNetworkIdle. The lower-level APIs do not automatically retry failed actions, and ordinary Vitest/Jest expect assertions are immediate unless wrapped in Vitest expect.poll or a custom eventually helper. Reliable HTMX tests therefore need domain-specific postcondition waits and must prohibit fixed sleeps.
reliability.flake_controls: Puppeteer supplies configurable default/action/navigation timeouts and deterministic event/condition waits. Vitest adds test/hook/teardown timeouts, retries with count/delay/error conditions, worker controls, bail, filters, and fixtures; Jest offers per-test timeouts and jest.retryTimes. Repeated whole-suite execution requires a script or CI loop. Retries should start fresh contexts and preserve first-attempt evidence instead of sharing a failed page, and database state must be reset before each attempt.
reliability.isolation_model: The recommended model is one worker-scoped Browser with a fresh BrowserContext and Page per test, closed through fixture cleanup, combined with unique or reset database state. A hard browser failure should recreate the worker/browser. Serial scenarios can intentionally share a context or database fixture, but that increases leakage risk. Vitest process/file isolation does not automatically isolate a separately shared Puppeteer Browser or PostgreSQL, so ownership must be explicit.
reliability.resource_usage: One Node runner plus a shared browser and per-test contexts is relatively economical; launching a browser per test is safer after crashes but slower. Each parallel worker/browser multiplies CPU and memory, while the default Linux Chrome download is about 282 MB plus chrome-headless-shell, Firefox, caches, videos, traces, and screenshots. Vitest's worker isolation also has process overhead. [uncertain] No Open Asset Allocator benchmark measured install disk, cold-start time, execution duration, peak memory, or the safe worker count.
reliability.parallelism_controls: Vitest runs files in parallel by default and supports maxWorkers, fileParallelism false, isolated pools, separate projects, and file-level --shard; projects can separate serial database tests from independent browser tests. Jest has maxWorkers, runInBand, projects, and sharding. Start the state-mutating E2E project with fileParallelism false or one worker, then increase only after assigning independent databases/schemas and artifact directories. Puppeteer itself does not schedule sessions or protect shared state.
reliability.flake_observability: Vitest's GitHub Actions summary identifies tests that passed only after retries, and JSON/JUnit/blob/custom reporters can retain attempt status; test context hooks can attach first-failure screenshots and logs. Jest reporters and retry hooks can expose similar data with more custom work. Neither Puppeteer nor these local runners supplies a long-term quarantine registry, historical flake dashboard, or root-cause classification. The repository must preserve attempt numbers, first-failure artifacts, repeat-run results, and trend data.

diagnostics_and_developer_experience.failure_artifacts: Puppeteer core can capture page/element screenshots, HTML content, console/page errors, request/response failures, Chrome performance traces, heap/coverage data, and WebM page screencasts when ffmpeg is installed. Its trace is a DevTools performance trace, not an action-by-action DOM snapshot trace. Nothing automatically starts, stops, or attaches these on test failure. Vitest annotations/file attachments or Jest custom reporters can associate files, but the fixture must collect them per attempt and ensure recorder/context closure.
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.debugging_tools: Developers can run headed, add slowMo, open DevTools, forward browser stdio with dumpio, log protocol traffic, inspect pending protocol calls, and debug Node code with --inspect-brk. Vitest adds file/name filters, watch mode, UI/HTML output, and IDE integration; Jest has mature watch and debugger workflows. There is no Puppeteer-specific step inspector, locator picker, automatic pause-on-failure, or Playwright-style time-travel trace viewer.
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.test_generation: Puppeteer core has no integrated recorder in the runner. Chrome DevTools Recorder can record browser flows and export/replay Puppeteer scripts through adjacent Puppeteer Replay tooling. Generated scripts are useful scaffolding but need conversion into Vitest/Jest tests, resilient locators, domain waits, fixtures, cleanup, and assertions before production use.
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.reporters: Vitest provides default/tree/verbose/dot/minimal, JSON, JUnit, TAP, HTML through @vitest/ui, GitHub Actions, blob, and custom reporters; blob reports support shard merging and attachments are handled separately. Jest provides console, JSON, custom reporters, and a large reporter ecosystem. Puppeteer contributes no reporter. The preferred Vitest stack can emit GitHub annotations and a job summary, but screenshots, traces, videos, and service logs must be explicitly attached and linked.
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.documentation_quality: Puppeteer has comprehensive, versioned API documentation and practical guides for installation, locators, browsers, protocols, Docker, request interception, and debugging. The docs accurately expose limitations such as no programmatic download handling and the difference between CDP and BiDi. Vitest and Jest runner docs are extensive. The composition lacks one authoritative E2E architecture guide, so lifecycle, fixture, retry-artifact, and database-isolation decisions remain spread across three projects and repository code.
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.local_workflow: With Vitest, developers can run one file or title filter, use watch mode or the UI, select a project/browser through configuration, disable file parallelism, and debug Node plus a headed browser. Puppeteer supports slow motion and DevTools. A project fixture can expose BASE_URL and browser choice. Keeping a failed browser open, replaying only a retry attempt, and viewing a unified browser/backend timeline require custom flags or hooks rather than a dedicated E2E UI.
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.failure_log_correlation: Page events can timestamp console messages, uncaught errors, requests, responses, and failures; Vitest task metadata supplies test identity and attachments. Gin, PostgreSQL, Flyway, and Docker Compose logs can be captured under the same run/test identifier in always-run workflow steps. Puppeteer and the runner do not correlate these processes automatically. The harness must establish UTC clocks, test/attempt IDs, log boundaries, artifact names, and capture ordering, especially for parallel workers.
diagnostics_and_developer_experience.artifact_data_exposure: Screenshots, videos, HTML, console output, response bodies, protocol logs, traces, downloads, and browser profiles can expose portfolio records, cookies, authorization headers, Yahoo responses, and credentials. NODE_DEBUG protocol logs are explicitly warned as sensitive. There is no universal redaction layer. Use synthetic data, fresh contexts, short restricted retention, selective network-body capture, header redaction, UI masking before screenshots where possible, and never upload cache/profile or unreviewed trace/video data by default.

github_actions_fit.official_ci_support: Puppeteer maintains installation/troubleshooting guidance and a versioned official GHCR image containing Chrome for Testing, dependencies, and Puppeteer. A normal GitHub-hosted Ubuntu job can use setup-node, npm ci, browser/system dependency installation, and vitest run. Vitest has documented GitHub Actions sharding/report merging and a built-in GitHub reporter. No dedicated Puppeteer GitHub Action is required, and application startup remains repository-specific.
github_actions_fit.browser_caching: Puppeteer caches managed browsers under $HOME/.cache/puppeteer by default, so GitHub Actions can cache that directory alongside npm's package cache. Keys should include OS, architecture, lockfile/Puppeteer version, and selected browser set. A restored browser must match the pinned Puppeteer revision; otherwise npx puppeteer browsers install should repair/populate it. The default Chrome payload is large, but caching must not preserve browser profiles or downloaded test data.
github_actions_fit.artifact_integration: Vitest can write JSON, JUnit, HTML, blob reports, annotations, and file attachments; Puppeteer artifacts can be placed in per-test attachment directories. GitHub actions/upload-artifact can upload reports, screenshots, traces, videos, diffs, downloads, and Compose logs under an always or not-cancelled policy. This is mechanically straightforward but not automatic: fixture hooks must create and annotate the files, and retention/access need a sensitive-data policy.
github_actions_fit.sharding_and_matrix_support: Vitest natively shards test files with --shard, emits blob reports, and merges them after GitHub matrix jobs; its documentation includes a complete Actions pattern. Browser projects or a matrix can select Chrome and Firefox. Puppeteer does not define projects or merge artifacts. Each shard/browser needs a unique database or must avoid state mutation, a unique artifact path, and deterministic file assignment. Jest also supports sharding, but this evaluation prefers Vitest's documented blob merge flow.
github_actions_fit.container_compatibility: Host-run Node/Puppeteer can test the repository's Docker Compose services through published ports on GitHub Ubuntu. The official Puppeteer image is versioned and includes Chrome dependencies, but its documented sandboxed invocation requests SYS_ADMIN and --init, so it should not be adopted blindly as a least-privilege CI default. If tests run in a container, localhost cannot reach host/other-container services without explicit networking. Shared memory, init, user/sandbox settings, image pinning, and service health checks require configuration.
github_actions_fit.failure_cleanup: Fixtures must stop screencasts/traces, close pages/contexts, and close or recreate the browser in finally/onCleanup hooks. Vitest's AbortSignal can react to test timeout or cancellation, but hard job cancellation can bypass Node teardown. GitHub Actions should collect logs first and then run docker compose down --volumes --remove-orphans under if: always(), delete downloads/artifacts according to retention, and use unique Compose project/volume names. Puppeteer has no application/database cleanup coordinator.

cost_and_risk.open_source_completeness: Puppeteer, Vitest/Jest, Chrome for Testing, Firefox, screenshots, screencasts, tracing, reporters, axe integration, and open-source image-diff libraries can provide the mandatory local and Linux CI capability without licensing fees. No hosted service is required. Completeness is achieved by composition and custom code rather than an integrated open-source E2E product, and native Safari is outside the stack.
cost_and_risk.optional_cloud_dependency: None for Chrome/Firefox execution, local reports, screenshots, video, accessibility checks, or sharding. Browser clouds and visual-review dashboards are optional for broader browser/device capacity, native Safari, analytics, and hosted baseline review. Local browser binaries, GitHub artifacts, committed image baselines, and Vitest/Jest reports provide non-cloud alternatives for the evaluated baseline, but not native Safari on Ubuntu.
cost_and_risk.migration_cost: Moderate. Tests use standard TypeScript, async/await, Node fetch, and familiar runner assertions, but page actions, locators, contexts, interception, traces, and browser setup bind to Puppeteer. Runner-neutral domain fixture APIs and page-object/helper boundaries can preserve scenario logic if moving to Playwright or WebDriver. Visual/lifecycle code is project-owned and may be reusable, but that ownership is also ongoing maintenance cost.
cost_and_risk.security_and_supply_chain: Puppeteer 25.8.0 has six direct npm dependencies in registry metadata, integrity signatures, and a SLSA provenance attestation published by GitHub Actions; Vitest 4.1.11 also exposes signatures/provenance, while Jest is an additional large dependency tree if selected. Installation downloads executable browser artifacts and Linux packages, introducing runtime egress and binary-update risk. Pin lockfiles and image digests/tags, verify npm integrity/provenance, scan dependencies/images, preserve the browser sandbox, restrict external URLs, and update quickly for browser security releases.
cost_and_risk.custom_harness_burden: High. The project must own Vitest/Jest configuration; browser/context/page fixtures; browser matrix; HTMX/Navigo waits; assertion polling; REST and PostgreSQL seed/reset; server-side Yahoo replacement; Compose/Flyway readiness and cleanup; programmatic download completion; visual baselines/diffs; retry-safe screenshot/video/trace collection; service-log correlation; artifact redaction; and database-safe parallelism. capability_delivery_tier.core_puppeteer: Chrome and Firefox control, CDP/BiDi transports, locators and actionability waits, browser contexts, input/navigation, device/environment emulation, request events/interception, screenshots, DevTools traces, screencasts, and browser downloads/management.
capability_delivery_tier.runner_vitest_or_jest: Discovery, assertions, hooks, fixtures or environments, timeouts, retries, worker limits, filters, projects, sharding, and machine-readable reports. Vitest is preferred for typed fixture scopes, attachments, blob merge, and GitHub reporting.
capability_delivery_tier.official_or_maintained_adjacent: Official Puppeteer Docker image and Chrome DevTools Recorder/Puppeteer Replay; maintained @axe-core/puppeteer accessibility audits; community image matchers and report viewers.
capability_delivery_tier.custom_repository_code: Application readiness and teardown, disposable PostgreSQL state, server-side external-service mocking, HTMX route postconditions, download completion/content checks, visual workflow, artifact capture/redaction/correlation, and safe browser/database sharding.
capability_delivery_tier.optional_paid_cloud: Native Safari/device capacity, hosted visual review, remote browser grids, and historical analytics; none is required for the Linux Chrome/Firefox baseline.

cost_and_risk.ai_execution_boundary: Puppeteer and Vitest/Jest execute deterministic committed code without an LLM, AI credentials, model egress, nondeterministic model choices, or per-run AI cost. Chrome DevTools Recorder is local deterministic recording rather than required AI. Optional AI authoring or MCP tools should remain outside required CI, use synthetic data and least privilege, and produce reviewed tests that continue to run when all AI services are unavailable.
